hints.title: Turn the supplied theorem into an exponent test
hints.body: Translate the supplied equivalence into a condition on each awkward prime exponent. Include exponent zero when a prime is absent.
hints.recap: Use the definition or the supplied equivalence directly; no proof of Fermat’s theorem is needed.
hints.pitfall: Zero is allowed as one of the two integers being squared.
hints.pause: Use the supplied test to examine the square claim.

recall.reminder: When a question supplies a definition, translate it into the exact conditions required before testing claims.

hints.title: Track one prime under multiplication
hints.body: Represent the exponents of one awkward prime in the two factors by integers; its product exponent is their sum.
hints.pitfall: The forward and reverse parity implications need separate checks.
hints.pause: Use the exponent sum to test both statements about products.

hints.title: Test a possible converse failure
hints.body: Test the possible parities of the two exponents and of their sum. If a reverse implication looks doubtful, choose actual factors that realise a failing parity case.
hints.recap: A parity condition on a sum need not determine both summands.
hints.pitfall: A proposed counterexample must satisfy the premise of the specific implication.
hints.pause: Construct and verify the factors and their product before assessing the converse claim.

recall.reminder: A parity condition on a sum need not determine both summands.

hints.title: Build the correcting multiplier
hints.body: List every awkward prime whose exponent obstructs the supplied condition. Decide how many additional copies of each are needed in the multiplier.
hints.recap: An existence construction must fix every obstruction.
hints.pitfall: Repairing only one problematic prime may leave another.
hints.pause: Construct the multiplier and assess the final claim before choosing the false statement.

recall.reminder: An existence construction must fix every obstruction.

solution:
A is true. Every positive square is a squaresum because N2=N2+02.

B is true. Multiplying numbers adds the exponent of each prime. If the two factors are squaresums, every awkward-prime exponent in each is even, including zero for an absent prime. Their product therefore also has only even awkward-prime exponents.

C is false. Set N=M=23. Neither factor is a squaresum because its awkward-prime exponent is 1, but NM=232 is a squaresum.

D is true. Choose k as the product of the awkward primes that occur to odd powers in N. Multiplication by k increases each of those powers by one and leaves every other awkward-prime power even. The supplied theorem then makes kN a squaresum.

The false statement is C.
knowledgePattern: Apply even-exponent criterion and disprove its factorwise converse
